en: Mālatī was abducted by Kapālakuṇḍalā and taken to Śrīparvata. There, Saudāmanī, a disciple of Kāmandakī, rebuked her and rescued Mālatī. Fearing for the misfortune of Mālatī’s kinsmen and Mādhava, Saudāmanī took the Vakula garland and returned swiftly from Śrīparvata. From that point begins the first act.

[Saudāmanī]: Because it is the abode of various supernatural powers (*siddhi*) and is of the nature of a deity, it is the "Lord’s Foot" (*bhagavatpada*). From Śrīparvata, there is a transition to Padmāvatī. (1) [C172/00] Regarding that: having heard that Mādhava—who could not bear the sight of the region familiar through his association with Mālatī—had abandoned his home and entered a rugged terrain connected to the mountains situated within the vast expanse of the interior of the great mountain range, [the audience hears] of him:

The connection is: "I shall follow close to Mādhava. (2) By saying "so be it," he intends to fly up to a great distance. Regarding mountains and so forth, "interference" (*vyatikara*) means an obstruction (*abhiṣaṅga*), such that one is completely enveloped by the eye; the meaning is that one enters into the interior of the orb of ocular light.

[1] Regarding *Padmāvatī*: the city of Padmāvatī is surrounded by the rivers named Sindhū and Pārā, which possess pure waters and are vast in extent. By way of these enclosures, it appears as if the sky itself has been rent asunder and cast down by the temples and other structures rising up from them. (XX) *Gopura* means a city gate; *aṭṭālāni* refers to houses constructed atop very high *stūpas*. (3) *Saṃghaṭṭa* means a dense conjunction.
Having split [the sky] in such a manner, it is released so specifically that it falls down, having become like a surrounding enclosure. (XX) [1]

[2] There is a river named Lavaṇā, the forest lands near which, during the rainy season, bring joy to the entire population of the country—that is, to all the people of the region. Of what nature are they? (XX) They possess a habit of bearing fresh *ulapa* garlands—that is, rows of grass—which are dear to pregnant cows. The short vowel occurs according to the rule: *iṣṭakeṣīkāmālānāṃ citatūlabhāriṣu*. In the compound *gogarbhiṇī*, the compound is formed by the rule *catuṣpādo garbhiṇyā*. (4) Likewise, they are "to be resorted to" (*sevyāḥ*), meaning they convey the pleasure of frequenting them. Thus, it is a three-word *karmadhāraya* compound. (5) [2]
The Indus falls from the mountain onto the earth; that waterfall, by its velocity and weight, has rent asunder the netherworld (*pātāla*).

(6) [3] *Tumula*: tumultuous, a confused noise like the roar of a great new cloud filled with water, which is fierce; in the "vicinity" (*paryanteṣu*), namely in the mountain thickets; in those, "resonance" (*vijṛmbhaṇam*) means the arising of an echo; therein, it attains a similarity of throat-sound with *Heramba*, that is, Gaṇapati. [3]

The word *prāyaḥ* means "mostly" or "for the most part. (7) *Pariṇataiḥ*: ripened; *mālūraiḥ*: by *bilva* fruits; [the waters are] fragrant. *Varuṇaḥ*: the *varuṇa* tree; in the forests of those [trees] and others, there are great bowers (*nikuñja*) in which the darkness is bound—that is, the darkness is confined—having been cast into the hollows of their bellies. In those deep, echoing caves (*gahvara*), there are outpourings—that is, echoes—in that Godāvarī river.

The mountain ranges have their expansive slopes made resonant by her; their state of sounding is due solely to echoes. And there is a recollection of the lightning because it dwells in the Deccan (*dakṣiṇāpatha*). The *Madhumatī* is a river, as is the *Sindhu*; the *saṃbheda* of these two is their confluence. By the term "non-human" (*apauruṣeya*), its beginninglessness is expressed.
(4) *Bhāvana* means production. *Nigama* means manifestation. (8) Its "supremacy" is due to its being the teacher even of teachers such as Viṣṇu (*Vaikuṇṭha*) and Brahmā (*Parameṣṭhin*). (9) [4]

[5] *Saṃsaktāḥ* (Continuous): Possessing continuity. A mountain whose high regions are darkened by fresh clouds; the sound of a peahen, vocal with joy, emitting a continuous cry; and trees inhabited by flocks of birds—by these, the paths are made lush, and they bestow delight upon the eyes. [5]

[6] "They bear" (*dadhati*). Herein: the growls (*ambūkṛtāni*)—that is, such indistinct roars—of young bears dwelling in the mountain caves, being amplified by their very location in the caves, bear a density (*styānam*), that is, a thickness. And the joints (*granthayaḥ*), which are the articulations of the *śallakī* trees—a species of tree whose fragrant sap is consumed by the elephants born in the mountains—which have been crushed (*dalitāḥ*) and pulverized by those elephants, and scattered (*vikīrṇāḥ*), cast here and there; these [joints] bear [that density].
Their outflow is the trickling of sap; by its touch it is cool, by its taste it is pungent and astringent, and its odor is such that it coagulates—that is, it spreads. (XX) [6]

[7] At that time, from the gambhārī tree toward the kṛtamāla tree—which possesses abundant shade due to its newly sprouted leaves—a bird known as a *koṇṭha* flies. And birds called *cāpa*, their beaks kissed by the pods—that is, the fruit-stalks—of the plants growing on the bank known as *virolī*, run toward the water. The qualification "on the bank of the *aśmantaka*" is used to illustrate their running on foot, owing to the absence of fear resulting from the lack of expected human traffic.

(XX) And by birds named *tāḍaka*, having entered well-concealed into the hollow of the trunk—the *prakāṇḍa* or stem of the *atimuktaka* tree, which extends from the root to the branches—they remained there, having made themselves secure. (10) Furthermore, following the warbling of those birds named *pāṇḍuka* who have made their nests among the creepers, birds called *kukkubha*, afflicted by the heat, utter their cries beneath the trees; such is the nature of their species. [7]

[Makaranda: [8] "Na yatra" (where not). For previously, the mind was sustained by hope regarding those calamities that had occurred—namely, the apprehension of Nanda’s marriage and so forth—but in this present calamity, it has been cast down.

Impelled thus, the mind does not rely upon hope, because no object of cognition is perceived that could serve as a basis for such hope—namely, the consolation provided by Āmandakī; nor does it abandon hope, because there is no certainty regarding its absence. Furthermore, when there arises a desire to know the cause that would determine either the positive or negative concomitance, it enters the darkness of delusion: it determines nothing at all.

(XX) "We, performing no purposeful action whatsoever, like those mounted on a wheel, failing to reach the next stage, turn back and once again find ourselves clinging to a state of indecision. (XX) Here the reason is: "Alas, when fate is adverse, how can there be a cessation of calamities? (XX) [8] [Mādhava: "Precisely because it is unknown, it is therefore marvelous; 'paryavasitā' means having reached completion. (XX) "Sambhāvanam" means consolation.

[9] “Priyamādhava” is a form of address. “Asi” means “you are. “Avatsalā” means one devoid of affection. “So ’ham eva” means: I am indeed that very person who, like a great festival incarnate, brought you joy with your hand. In what manner? By personally requesting the taking of the marriage bracelet (*kaṅkaṇa*). For even another who brings joy likewise takes the bracelet. (XX) [9]

[10] "Sarasa" means that due to her extreme delicacy, she was unable to endure physical pressure. "From this" means from what will be stated immediately hereafter. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "What more [can be said]? Therefore we say. (XX) The meaning is that the torment of love had reached such a supreme pitch that she fell under the sway of a rash resolve unsuitable for a woman of noble family. [10]

[11] In the context of the proposal for the marriage at Nandana, she—whose heart was agitated by piteous compassion, devoid of fortitude yet flowing with the essence of mercy; who, through her distress, was disoriented and unsettled—expressed, that is, expanded, her intention consisting of affection toward me. "Taraṅgita" means moved from its natural state. [11]

[12] *Dalati*: it is split open; it is rent asunder. "Becoming twofold" refers to the state prior to the splitting; likewise, in the subsequent cases as well, when the preceding uninterrupted state has manifested, there is a delay in the succeeding state. (XX) By the first half-verse, the two internal calamities (*adhyātmika-vipat*) are described; by the third, the external calamity (*ādhibhautikī vipat*); and by the fourth, the celestial or supernatural calamity (*adhidaivikī*).
[12] [Makaranda: *Avagrahaḥ*: obstruction. *Parisare*: in the surrounding regions.

[13] *Unnāla* means: at the end of summer, because there is very little water, there are young lotus-beds with stalks (*nāla*) emerging from the lake; the flow of their nectar—the stream of floral juice—is its *saṃvalana*, which is its mixing together. With that, the fragrance is *māṃsala*, meaning abundant. Its *bandhu* is its companion. Of the *parivartamāna* waves—those oscillating by the force of the wind—the *śīkara* is the scattered spray of water drops; that itself is the *nīhāra*, the frost.
By that, it is *jaḍa*, meaning cold. (11) [13]
[Makaranda: "I distract him; I make him preoccupied with something else.

[14] Regarding the phrase "In this": "With intoxication" means with joy; "sweet-voiced" means possessing an indistinctly sweet sound; that which is a "mallikākṣa" is a swan whose beak and feet are dark. Because they are shaken by its two wings, the white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*) therein are "throbbing," meaning they are active, and possess high stalks. He says this because of the continuous, protracted weeping: "How will he see that?"—referring to the falling away of one previously arisen flood of tears and the emergence of another.
"Beginning" (*prārambha*) refers to the interval between these two beginnings of falling. "Divisions" (*vibhāgāḥ*) means parts (*pradeśāḥ*). [14] [Makaranda:

"Lack of apprehension" (*apratipattiḥ*) means lack of attention; by that, "voidness" (*śūnyatā*), meaning the absence of consciousness (*caitanyavirahaḥ*), serves as a qualifier for the action of rising.

[15] In the groves (*nikuñja*)—that is, in the thickets of creepers and the like—the waters of those rivers have their scent clinging to them through the growth of *vānīra* reeds, namely the flowers of the fragrant cane. The *yūthikā* is well known as the *prahī*; its *sumanas*—its flowers—are in the state of *jālaka*, meaning buds or sheaths of blossoms, designated by the term *kṣāraka*, which have "opened up" (*ujjṛmbhita*), that is, have begun to swell. The meaning is that they have abandoned the state of being buds and have transformed into the state of full-blown flowers.

Furthermore, on the precipices well-known as Karātas, because the clouds resting there act like canopies, the peacocks perform their *tāṇḍava* dances upon the ridges. In *tāṇḍava* dances, offerings such as heaps of flowers, sprinkling of water, and canopies are performed. With this intention, it was said: "in those beautiful with the laughter-like form of blooming *kuṭaja* flowers. [15]

[16] *Jṛmbheti*. By "expansion" (*vikāśena*), that is, by blossoming, there is the *jarjara*—the withered—*ḍimba*, which is like a *golaka* (a spherical cluster). The *ḍambara* of such [clusters] is their grand display of maturity (*prauḍhiprapañca*). Those [mountain regions] in which such *kadamba* trees are *ghana*—dense and continuous—and *śrīmat*—possessing extraordinary beauty—are mountain-expanses of that kind. (XX) And the quarters of the sky are darkened by the *kādambinī*—a row of clouds. A *kādambinī* consists of the females (*yoṣitaḥ*) of *kādamba*s, that is, of *kalahaṃsa* swans.

Because of these [qualities], the Kashmiris call them "dark" (*śyāmalā*). "With emerging" means with breaking forth; "with *kandalas*" means with new sprouts; "lovely" means beautiful; those are the *ketaka* trees; "bearing them" refers to the banks (*kacchāḥ*) of the river currents (*saritsrotasām*), that is, the riverbanks. "Manifesting fragrance" means whose scents are becoming evident; by those *śilīndhra* and *lodhra* flowers, the "row" (*tatiḥ*)—meaning the garland—of forests appears as if "smiling," as if possessed of a smile. *Śilīndhra* is a specific type of tree that blossoms during the rainy season.

[Mādhava: Those things whose objects are beautiful yet difficult to behold; they are thus described. And their quality of being "difficult to behold" arises from their serving as excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) for the state of separation (*vipralambha*).

[17] *Utphulleti*. That eastern, fierce wind which blows, scented by two blossoming *arjuna* and *śāla* trees; by that [wind], there is a swaying: swaying means oscillation. By that, the rows of clouds—smooth like sapphire and like the horns of a buffalo (the meaning of the word *gavala*)—have become unsteady: displaced from their positions. (XX) And they are permeated with a fragrance intensified by the sprinkling of the earth scorched by the summer heat.

"By the departure and arrival of heat and water" refers to them respectively. That is to say, the departure of heat and the arrival of water—such is the nature of the *vyatikara*, which means an intermingling. Those days have the quality (*śīla*) of bearing the splendor associated with that [intermingling]. (13) [17]

[18] In the reading *kathaṃ paśyāmi kakubhaḥ*, the meaning is: those [directions] in which there are dense clouds, dark as young *tamāla* trees, rising—that is, ascending—and which possess the *heti*, the weapon, namely the bow of *Hari* (Indra), and so forth; this is easily understood. However, in the reading *saritaḥ*, the connection with the clouds is established through their reflection. Likewise, *hareḥ* refers to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva; his *heti* is the discus (*cakra*), and birds bearing that name [the *cakravākas*] inhabit them.
*Kalaha* here signifies mere clamor. (XX) [18]

[Makaranda: *Daśā* (state): a condition presided over by a planet. *Vinoda* (diversion): that which brings peace to the mind. *Paryavasitaprāyā* (almost finished): nearly completed. *Pramugdha* (stupefied): unconscious. *Anukrośa* (pity): compassion. [19] *Apahastitabāndhave*: one who has cast aside her kinsmen; an address to her as "O you who have rejected your relatives. *Tṛṣṇā* (thirst): greed. The meaning is: "Having even abandoned your kinsmen, you yourself committed this rash act of offering your hand out of greed; why now are you so merciless? *Krama* (order): sequence. [19]
*Ucchvāsaḥ*: the recovery of consciousness.

[20] *Mātar mātar* and so forth is *pralāpa* (incoherent speech). *Dalati*: it splits; that is to say, it bursts asunder. "O mother, O mother! is weeping (*rudita*). "The heart splits" is lamentation (*vilapita*). This is the *abhinaya* (gestural representation) of despondency (*nirveda*). *Dhvaṃsate*: it becomes slackened. *Dehabandhaḥ*: the joints of the limbs. And this is the *abhinaya* denoting the drooping of the body. "I consider myself empty" is the *abhinaya* of the *sāttvika-bhāva* known as *pralaya* (fainting). "With incessant flames" is the *abhinaya* of anxiety (*cintā*).

"Sinking in blind darkness" is an expression of exhaustion. "Vidhura" means without support. "Moha," however, is expressed by its own term. (XX) "Viṣvak" means on all sides. "Sthagayati" means it causes the delusion of all the senses; this is the meaning. "Katham" refers to what ought to be done. (XX) That too is of the very nature of delusion. [20] [21] "Bandhutā": in the hearts of the circle of kinsmen and in the eyes of Mālatī, he is a charming (*mugdha*)—that is, a young—moon, a cause of joy (*nandana*). This too is an elaboration of her lamentations. [21]

[22] "Ānanda" means bliss itself; that which has bliss as its very form. "By Time" (kālena) means by Death (Antaka). "Tearing away" (uddharatā) means leading [him] away after severing him from his kinsmen.

[22] [23] "Give" (vitara) means bestow. "Makaranda is dear to you"; therefore, look upon me, your own friend, and speak with me. "Why do you not regard me? means why do you not accept me? [23] [Makaranda: "One whose complexion" (chaviḥ)—meaning luster—is "radiant" (rucirā), meaning brilliant, and "full" (māṃsalā), meaning thick. "Downpour" (āsāraḥ) means a torrential rain.

[Mādhava: [24] In the northern direction of a river whose slender ripples have been checked—having their course obstructed—as they pass through a thicket of *jambu* trees that are intensely dark due to the ripening (the maturation) of their fruit-bearing loads; the thinness of the ripples being due to the lack of entry of strong winds into the thicket. Mature *tāpiccha* or *tamāla* trees, possessing dense and thick rows, are likewise dark blue.

By means of its novelty, he intends to express an excellence of blackness. Because her body possesses an extreme blackness in every direction, it is the rainy season itself that is thus described. (XX) [24]

[25] "Kac cit" is used for making an inquiry. "Saumyaḥ" means gentle, because it bestows joy upon the eyes. "Praṇayaḥ" is affection characterized by trust. "Paurastyaḥ" means originating from the eastern direction. "Sādhusaṃvāhanābhiḥ" means by means of gentle massages. It is well known in the world that even another person with a good companion performs a massage in the form of grasping the feet with the fist and so forth. "Viṣvak" means on all sides. "Surapatidhanuḥ" is the jeweled bow (the rainbow). "Bibhrat" means bearing this, which is "lakṣmīvat," endowed with splendor.

"Dadhāna" is an address to the cloud; according to his own desire, Mādhava thus inquires of the cloud regarding the excellence of his beloved’s friends and attendants. (14) [25] Immediately following this inquiry, he says "This," considering the thundering of the cloud to be a response. "Utkaṇṭhāḥ": with necks upraised. "Mandram": deep and sweet. "Anumananam": conversing. "Bhagavan": the attribution of divinity due to the intensity of his distress. "Jīmūtaḥ": a cloud.

[26] By saying "by fate," he shows that the possibility of seeing her has been swallowed up by improbability. The sense is that it is not conceivable that she could have remained alive until this time. By using the word "world" (*jagati*), he indicates the excellence of her beauty and charm. By addressing him as "Your Honor" (*sa bhavān*), he wins over the messenger with a term of respect. By saying "Mālatī, my beloved," because she is his dear one, he reveals her inability to endure the agony of separation due to the indication of her fresh delicacy.

At the beginning, there is consolation, intended to provide even a slight measure of mental composure following the hearing of the news. "The state of Mādhava" is an expression meant to demonstrate the extreme intensity of her inability to endure [his absence] due to her affection. "The thread of hope" is the support for her life. "Exceedingly," etc.

This condition of mine must be described by means of the Middle Way (*madhyamā vidhi*); for otherwise, the heroine, whose heart is intensely attached to me, might perceive an absence of affection in me due to my perceived hardness of heart and immediately abandon her life out of despair. Or, even considering the calamity of being consumed by the unbearable heat of the fire of separation, she might remain in that very state, hopeless of me. (XX) "By some means" (*katham api*) means with great difficulty.

"In that case, even a mere thread of hope is sufficient for the protection against such calamities for one who is so exceedingly delicate. (XX) By the words "of the long-eyed one," he describes how, among those possessing physical form, there exists a descent and an elevation that surpass all others. (15) By the words "that very one," he says that no other path exists; this is the "confusion" mentioned here. (16) His state of being joyful arises from the conceit that he has set out after accepting my word. For this very reason, he says "Ah! Moving elsewhere serves to indicate a lack of delight in staying in one place due to extreme distress.

[Makaranda: It is indeed madness that acts as an eclipse—a seizing by Rāhu—assailing Mādhava himself, who is like the moon, because his sight is the nectar for the eyes of the world. Because his father and others were well-accustomed to him during childhood when he entered into states of distress, and because that state has not been long past, there is a recollection of his father and the rest. "O Blessed One" is a cry directed toward Kāmandakī.
[Mādhava: "Pramāda" means lack of attention. "Dhik" means alas! how painful!

[27] "In new [trees]" (*naveṣu*): because in ancient ones, dryness has manifested. Others hold that since the introduction was made with a qualification (*saviśeṣaṇam*) while the formal composition (*upanibandhana*) is without qualification (*nirviśeṣaṇam*), it would be inconsistent; therefore, "in new" is a term in a different grammatical case (*vyadhikaraṇa*), not a qualification of another word. (17) *Pramathya*: having killed. *Vibhaktā*: held after being cut into pieces. By saying "in the forest" (*vipine*), the suitability of the location for the ease of slaughtering living beings is stated. [27]

[Makaranda: [28] "In a friend," and so forth, with the locative case used in the sense of "in" (*satsaptamī*). (18) "In a friend" means in one whose heart is stainless. "In a beloved" means in me, who am dear. To the question, "How indeed was such friendship brought to fulfillment? he replies, "In childhood play. "Matured" means having reached its full development. "Named Mālatī"—separation from her; the mental anguish resulting from that is itself the disease; in one bearing the onset of that [disease]. (19) "Having shattered" means having burst open—by this common expression, the meaning is that it did not depart by any means. (XX) [28]

[Mādhava]: Mādhava refutes the initial meaning of the verse beginning with "naveṣu" by suggesting the possibility of an alternative explanation, stating "sulabhā. (XX) The passage beginning with "Ayam ahaṃ bhoḥ" is an elaboration on the intensity of his speed. (20) By the phrase "for a moment, by bestowing attention," the smallness of what is requested is expressed.

[29] “With all her limbs” (*sarvāṅga*) reveals the uncommon nature of her supernatural knowledge (*abhijñā*). By describing her as a noble lady (*kulavadhū*), there is a refutation of the suspicion that she might be a wanton woman (*lampaṭā*). “By those staying here” (*ihasthaiḥ*) expresses the possibility of her frequenting this place. Through the two uses of the particle *vā*, it is stated that seeing her and learning her history yield equal results. “The union of youth” (*vayassaṃdhi*) refers to the stage of life. While passion (*madana*) acts boldly within the heart, it is timid (*apragalbha*) in the body, for she is still charming (*mugdha*). (XX) [29]

"Alas! How painful!"—thus, through the excitants (*uddīpanavibhāva*) to be expounded in the subsequent group of verses, he manifests his own mental anguish, the heroine's precarious state of life, and the futility of his words of supplication, because she does not listen to him despite his addressing her.

[30] He demonstrates that very same failure to listen (*anākarṇana*) through various modes, beginning with "by means of *kekā* cries. "With his crest raised" (*ucchikhaṇḍaḥ*) means having his plumage tossed upward. "Intoxication itself" (*mada eva*) refers to the state of being arrogant with passion; from that very state comes the rapid whirling of the eyes. By the word "approaches" (*abhisarati*), it is indicated that the beloved belongs to another. Consequently, due to the intensity of the impulse of desire, there is a failure to listen. "Golāṅgūla" is a black-faced monkey. "Chūraṇam" means painting or coloring. "Inopportune" (*anavasara*) because living beings are attached elsewhere. [30]

[31] *Valīvadana* means a monkey. *Kāmpilya* means the *rohiṇī* tree; the suffix *-ka* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). *Prasava* means a flower. *Pālī* means a mound or plot of ground. *Pāka* refers to both the internal and external [process of ripening]. [31] *Rohiṇānokaha* means the *rohaḍa* tree. (22)

[32] It is a natural law that when a female elephant has her temple scratched by the tip of a tusker’s tusk, her eyes become closed like buds. (XX) "Scratching" means rubbing. And she provides for her own sustenance—that is, her maintenance—by feeding on half-chewed fresh shoots of the *śallakī* tree. "Boldness" refers to engaging in free conversation through the act of moving back and forth, swaying, and oscillating while describing [the tusker] with great eloquence. (XX) [32]

[33] *Āmandram*: slightly deep. *Udbhaṭagarjitam*: a loud roar. *Āvarjitaiḥ*: accepted. *Dānajyāniḥ*: the loss of rut; the despondency caused by that; the bee that has become mute due to that despondency; by its *vyāsaṅgena* (attachment/absorption), meaning by being preoccupied with something else, his face became *dīnam* (dejected/sorrowful)—he who is thus described. *Nūnam* expresses the manifestation of one's own experience. *Vidhuraḥ*: overwhelmed. *Stamberamaḥ*: an elephant. [33]

The single qualification of the lake is that it is "fragrant with the falling of freshly blossomed *kadamba* flowers. Likewise, there is the "cool fragrance," meaning an exceedingly lovely scent; it is "dense" (*bahala*), meaning abundant; "concentrated" (*saṃgalita*), meaning gathered together in one place; and "full-bodied" (*māṃsala*), meaning thick. This [fragrance] is combined with the "flow from the temples"—that is, rut—which has "smeared the cheeks. Furthermore, it is mixed with the "scattered fragments" of a cluster of lotuses that have been "thoroughly crushed" (*samuddalita*), meaning well-pounded.

Scattered [are] the very petals of the lotus-pond, as well as the lotuses, their filaments, the lotus-stalks, and the roots of the *viśa* plant; likewise, there are tender sprouts and other things—this is another [verse]. (23) Another [verse] begins with "Anavarata" and ends with "nīhāra. Another begins with "Uttrasta" and ends with "sārasa. *Anuvṛtti* means service.

[34] *Cheda* means cessation (*virati*). *Puṣkara* means lotus (*padma*). *Gaṇḍūṣasaṃkrānti* means the act of giving water by placing one's own trunk, filled with water in that manner, into the mouth of the female elephant (*kariṇī*). *Anarāla* means straight (*akuṭila*). [34]

[35] *Ucchvasitavaiśasam*: the agony of sustaining life, such as this. Even elsewhere, solitude alone is the cause. (24) If it is asked, "Who else is to be expected? he says in response: "May that day perish which does not exist in your company, O Makaranda, and in hers—that is, in the company of Mālatī. (XX) *Pramodamṛgatṛṣṇikā*: a false joy; of what kind? Because of the reason that [such joy exists] elsewhere only among humans. (25) [35]

[Makaranda: By the words "the lord of my life," he has said: "Only while you live do I truly live. (XX) He is one whose longing—that is, the eagerness—for my embrace has become manifest. *Pariccheda* means certainty.

(36) All that fear—accompanied by trembling even without a specific cause—which was constantly experienced by my heart, which was filled with the heat of affection and ever counting your misfortunes, is now, in this single moment, brought to its conclusion for me. IX, 19–20 19. When the mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, devoid of defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, it is turned toward the knowledge of the recollection of past lives. He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of world-dissolution, many aeons of world-evolution, many aeons of world-dissolution and evolution: "There I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, such a lifespan; passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere, and there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, such a lifespan; passing away from there, I was reborn here. Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details. 20. When the mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, devoid of defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, it is turned toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma: "These beings, on account of misconduct of body, speech, or mind, or of holding wrong views, have been reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell; these beings, on account of good conduct of body, speech, or mind, or of holding right views, have been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Thus with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.
